library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(mosaic)
library(infer)
library(caret)


hook_output = knit_hooks$get('output')
knit_hooks$set(output = function(x, options) {
  # this hook is used only when the linewidth option is not NULL
  if (!is.null(n <- options$linewidth)) {
    x = xfun::split_lines(x)
    # any lines wider than n should be wrapped
    if (any(nchar(x) > n)) x = strwrap(x, width = n)
    x = paste(x, collapse = '\n')
  }
  hook_output(x, options)
})

```

# Tree-based machine learning methods
## Tree-Based Methods

- Can be used for both regression and classification
  + Regression models $\longrightarrow$  quantitative response variable

  + Classification models $\longrightarrow$ categorical response 


- These involve stratifying or segmenting the predictor space into a number of simple regions


# Example Classification Scenario
## Example: Marijuana legalization

The General Social Survey is a wide-ranging survey conducted biannually to measure cultural shifts in American society. We can use the GSS to get an idea of how popular opinion has changed. 

**Goal**: Use Age to predict people’s opinion of marijuana legalization.


```{r, echo = FALSE}
GSS <- read.csv("GSS2016.csv")

table(GSS$GRASS)
```

::: {.notes}
Data Cleanings Steps (see `decision-trees-random-forests.R`)
- Only going to look at one year, 2016, and remove "Not applicable" from our response
- Want just two groups for responses: Legal and Not legal
- Change variables to proper type (numeric - will have coercion)
:::


## Let's Clean Our Data! Yay!

Data: [GSS2016.csv](GSS2016.csv)  
Data cleaning: [`decision-trees-random-forests.R`](decision-trees-random-forests.R)

- Let's only look at one year, say 2016, and remove "Not applicable from our response"
- Want just two groups for responses: Legal and Not legal
- Change variables to proper type

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "1-3|4-5|6"
GSS <- GSS %>%
  filter(YEAR==2016) %>%
  filter(GRASS != 'Not applicable')
GSS <- GSS %>%
  mutate(LEGAL = ifelse(GRASS=='Legal', 'Legal', 'Not legal'))
GSS$AGE <- as.numeric(GSS$AGE)
```


## Testing data v. Training data

```{r}
set.seed(4)
test_id <- sample(1:nrow(GSS), size=round(0.2*nrow(GSS)))
TEST <- GSS[test_id,]
TRAIN <- GSS[-test_id,]
```

How many people in the training data set support marijuana legalization?

```{r}
TRAIN %>% group_by(LEGAL) %>% summarize(n=n())
```



# Decision Trees: Classification
## What is a decision tree

Decision trees: A tree-like model of decisions and their possible consequences

- Has flowchart-like structure in which each...

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align='left',out.width="75%", fig.alt="Overview of the flowchart structure of a decision tree. The tree begins at a root decision node. Based on the test outcome of this decision node, this leads to other outcomes. These tests keep happening until we reach a terminal node of the decision tree which provides the predicted outcome."}

knitr::include_graphics("./images/decision-tree.png")

```


## How Decision Trees classify



How to decide to split?

- As the number of predictors increases, so does the number of possible trees.
  + Optimal decision trees do not exist (Hyafil & Rivest, 1976)
  + So several competing methods for building decision trees


## How Decision Trees classify (cont)

Recursive Partitioning: Split infinite # of times until reach stopping criterion.

Split:

- Gini Index (default): $$G = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat{p}_{mk}(1-\hat{p}_{mk})$$ where $\hat{p}_{mk}$ is the proportion of training observations in $m^{th}$ region from $k^{th}$ class.
    
Stop:

- Complexity parameter

  

## Fitting A Decision Tree (Classification)

```{r}
#install.packages('rpart')
library(rpart)
rpart(LEGAL~AGE, data=TRAIN, na.action = na.pass)
```


## Visualizing a Decision Tree (Classification)

```{r, message=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=10, eval = FALSE}

#install.packages("rattle")
library(rattle)
tree <- rpart(LEGAL~AGE, data=TRAIN, na.action = na.pass)
fancyRpartPlot(tree)
```


```{r, echo = FALSE}
tree <- rpart(LEGAL~AGE, data=TRAIN, na.action = na.pass)

```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center',out.width="75%", fig.alt="Decision tree for GSS data with just Age as an explanatory variable. There is a split at Age = 69, where those younger than 69 are classified as Legal, and those 69 and older are classified as Not Legal"}

knitr::include_graphics("./images/tree1.png")

```

# Evaluation
## Evaluating a decision tree

- Confusion Matrix
- Classification Accuracy


## Evaluating a decision tree: Confusion Matrix

```{r}
TRAIN <- TRAIN %>%
  mutate(Legal_Tree = predict(tree, type='class'))

confusion_train <- tally(Legal_Tree~LEGAL, data=TRAIN)
confusion_train
```

```{r}
TEST <- TEST %>%
  mutate(Legal_Tree = predict(tree, type='class', newdata = TEST))

confusion_test <- tally(Legal_Tree~LEGAL, data=TEST)
confusion_test
```


## Evaluating a decision tree: Classification Accuracy

Training Accuracy:

```{r}
sum(diag(confusion_train))/nrow(TRAIN)
```

Testing Accuracy:

```{r}
sum(diag(confusion_test))/nrow(TEST)
```



## Tuning Parameter: Complexity parameter

Using recursive partitioning can overfit the training data - Prune Tree 

```{r, message=FALSE}
printcp(tree)
```

- Changing complexity parameter:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#| code-line-numbers: "2"
rpart(LEGAL~AGE, data=TRAIN, na.action = na.pass,
      control = rpart.control(cp = 0.05))
```


# Decision Trees for Regression
## Decision Trees (Regression)




How to decide to split?

- Find regions $(R_j)$ that minimizes the residual sum of squares $$RSS = \sum^{J}_{j=1}\sum_{i \in R_j}(y_i - \hat{y}_{R_j})^2$$
  - Stops when you reach some criterion (cp)



## Fitting A Decision Tree (Regression)

Let's suppose we want to use people’s political view (POLVIEWS) and marital status (MARITAL) to estimate people’s age.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tree2 <- rpart(AGE~POLVIEWS+MARITAL, data=TRAIN)
fancyRpartPlot(tree2)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tree2 <- rpart(AGE~POLVIEWS + MARITAL, data=TRAIN)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center',out.width="75%", fig.alt="A regression decision tree with an initial split for Marital status. For those who were never married or separated have a predicted age of 32. For those who are married or divorced, they have a predicted age of 52. Anyone in a different category has a predicted age of 69."}

knitr::include_graphics("./images/tree2.png")

```


## Prediction using Decision Tree

We can still use the predict function to predict our regression decision tree outputs. 
```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "1-3|1"
TEST <- TEST %>% filter(MARITAL != "No answer") 

predict(tree2, TEST , method = "anova") %>% head()
```


**Be Careful**: Can only predict using categorical variables located in the Training Set

# Comparison with other methods
## Trees Versus Linear Models

- If the relationship between the features and the response is well approximated by
a linear model: 
  + Linear regression 
  
<br>
<br>

- If instead there is a highly nonlinear and complex relationship between the features and the response as indicated by model: 
  + Decision trees

# Random Forests
## Random Forests

A random forest is collection of decision trees that are aggregated by majority rule

  
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>

When to use random forest:




## Building a Random Forest

In building a random forest, each time a split in a tree is considered, a random sample of *m* predictors is chosen as split candidates from the full set of *p* predictors. 

<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>


Hence, at each split in the tree, the algorithm is not even allowed to consider a majority of the available predictors. Why is this a good thing?


## Random Forests 

**Example**: Which variables are most important for predicting views on marijuana legalization?


```{r, message=FALSE}
#install.packages('randomForest')
library(randomForest)

forest_grass <- randomForest(as.factor(LEGAL)~NEWSFROM+HAPPY+RELIG+COURTS+
                             ENERGY+EDUC+ENVIR+POLVIEWS+PARTYID+REGION+
                             INCOME+SEX+DEGREE+AGE+MARITAL+BALLOT,data=TRAIN,
                             na.action = na.omit, ntree=201, mtry=4)

forest_grass
```


## Random Forests: Prediction

```{r}
TEST <- TEST %>%
  mutate(Legal_RF = predict(forest_grass, type='class', 
                            newdata = TEST)) 

TEST$Legal_RF[1:5]

confusion_test <- tally(Legal_RF~LEGAL, data=TEST)
sum(diag(confusion_test))/nrow(TEST)
```


## Variable Importance

Since each tree in a random forest uses a different set of variables, we want to keep track of which variables seem to be the most consistently influential. 

.tiny[
```{r}
randomForest::importance(forest_grass) %>% as.data.frame() %>% 
  rownames_to_column() %>% arrange(desc(MeanDecreaseGini))
```

# Summary 
## Modeling Data {.smaller}

- [**Linear model**](../../08-statistical-foundations/slides/linear-models/linear-models.html)
  + The basic model for *regression* only
  + easy interpretation, but strict assumptions
  + Use [cross-validation (CV)](../../09-cv-and-knn/slides/cv.html) to ensure quality of model
  <!-- + thus hard to get a better prediction -->

- [**KNN:**](../../09-cv-and-knn/slides/knn.html)
  + Can be applied to *regression* and *classification*
  + fast, no assumptions, can add data anytime.
  + large number of variables can lower quality
  + use CV to decide $k$

- **Decision tree:**
  + Can be applied to *regression* and *classification.*
  + good data visualization 
  + high variance

- **Random Forest:**
  + a collection of tree models; can be applied to *regression*^[This is uncommon, though] and *classification.*
  + Hard to interpret, but can output variable importance
    + Can be useful for *variable selection*
  + outperforms linear model when variables are no linearly independent
